questions.explanation: Options A and D were common wrong answers, and the report says most candidates did not appear to understand the term mechanical working. Mechanical working is a force moving something through a distance. A stone falling from a building is that: gravity acts on it as it moves, and energy is transferred from the gravitational store to the kinetic store. A is electrical working, C is energy carried by radiation and D is heating by conduction. Answer: B. When a question names a type of transfer, match each option to its name.

Many candidates chose C, believing the energy transferred depends on the time taken. The energy transferred by a force is the work done, force × distance moved in the direction of the force: Fd, option A. Dividing by t gives power, which is option C. The time in the question is extra information. Check the unit: newtons times metres is joules, with no seconds in it.

Most candidates thought the reading fell because cotton wool is an insulator, and chose B. Insulation cannot explain a reading below room temperature: it would only slow any warming. Something has to carry energy away. The alcohol evaporates. The most energetic molecules escape from the surface, so the average energy of the molecules left behind falls and the thermometer cools: D.

Many candidates used the correct equation but did not convert kilohertz into hertz. 340 / 1.2 = 283, which is option C (280 m). Some converted correctly and then divided the frequency by the wave speed: 1200 / 340 = 3.5, which is option B. The equation is v = fλ, so λ = v / f = 340 / 1200 = 0.28 m: A. Convert the prefix first: 1.2 kHz = 1200 Hz.

Option B was the common wrong answer. The report says many candidates thought the vibrations in light are parallel to the direction the wave travels. That describes a longitudinal wave, like sound. Light is a transverse wave, so the vibrations are at right angles to the direction of travel. Direction RS is along the beam, so it is ruled out. WX and YZ are both perpendicular to the beam: C.

Most candidates did not recall that the angles of incidence and reflection are measured between the ray and the normal. Many chose B, 50°, which is the angle printed on the diagram. That 50° is between the ray and the mirror surface. The normal is at 90° to the mirror, so the angle of incidence is 90 − 50 = 40°. The angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence: A. Draw the normal before you read any angle.

Most candidates knew that the image formed from sunlight by a converging lens is real. Many thought it would be enlarged, and chose B. The Sun is so far away that its rays arrive effectively parallel, and the lens brings them to a point at the principal focus. That makes a tiny bright image, much smaller than the Sun. Real and diminished: A.

The report says most candidates knew the order of red, green and violet in the visible spectrum, but the majority of those could not put them in order of increasing wavelength. Option A runs the wrong way round. Violet has the shortest wavelength and red the longest, with green between them: violet, green, red, which is D. Learn the spectrum with the labels attached: the red end is long wavelength and low frequency, the violet end is short wavelength and high frequency.

The report found answers spread across all four options, suggesting many candidates guessed, and that most chose an option where the wavelength decreased. The question says that expansion of the Universe makes the wavelength of the waves reaching the Earth increase. So the waves must move to a part of the spectrum with a longer wavelength. Radio to microwaves, microwaves to ultraviolet and microwaves to gamma rays all go to shorter wavelengths. Visible light to microwaves goes to longer wavelengths: C.

Option A was the common wrong answer. The report says most candidates worked out that rod 2 was aluminium, which is not affected by the magnet. Many were confused about magnetised steel. Magnetised steel is a magnet, so it attracts to one pole and repels from the other. Rod 1 attracts to both poles, which is what an unmagnetised piece of iron does, because the magnet induces magnetism in it. Rod 1 is iron and rod 2 is aluminium: D.

Most candidates recalled that the core of an electromagnet is iron. Many then chose A, believing an electromagnet is a permanent magnet. It is not. Iron is magnetised when there is a current in the coil and loses almost all of its magnetism when the current is switched off, so the electromagnet is a temporary magnet. That is why a crane can release the scrap it lifts. Answer: B.

Most candidates recognised that the pointer would deflect. Some chose C, thinking the needle would then stay put and give a steady reading. The sphere holds a limited amount of charge and is not connected to a battery. Charge flows to earth through the ammeter until the sphere has none left, then the current stops. The pointer deflects and then returns to zero: B.

Most candidates worked out the resistance of the two resistors as if they were in series, 3.0 + 6.0 = 9.0 Ω, which is option C. They are in parallel: 1/R = 1/3.0 + 1/6.0 = 1/2.0, so R = 2.0 Ω: A. A quick check: the combined resistance of resistors in parallel is always smaller than the smallest one, so only 2.0 Ω can be right.

The report says most candidates thought the magnetic field around a solenoid is circular, and chose A. A circular pattern belongs to a straight wire. A solenoid has the field of a bar magnet: along the axis through the coil, out of one end, round the outside and back in at the other end. So the compasses at the ends point along the axis, and the ones beside the coil point the opposite way to the field inside. In D the end compasses both point left and the side compasses both point right: D. The report adds that some candidates saw the ends were towards or away from the solenoid but gave the sides the same direction.
